source_title: Why Germans won't buy a round of beer From Berlin bars to Bavarian beer gardens, who pays for what is taken seriously in Germany. Here's why splitting the bill can actually be a sign of friendship.
source_excerpt:
From Berlin bars to Bavarian beer gardens, who pays for what is taken seriously in Germany. Here's why splitting the bill can actually be a sign of friendship.
Picture the scene: you're travelling through Germany and have gone out to dinner with a new group of local friends. Everyone has eaten, had a drink or two and shared plenty of laughs.
There is no "let's just split it". Instead, the first person tells the waiter exactly what they ordered – spaghetti and two beers – and pays precisely that amount. The next pays for their pizza and glass of wine. And so it goes, right around the table.
Ute Junker is an award-winning journalist who was born in Australia to German parents and went to school in both countries. She has edited magazines in both Australia and Germany and writes frequently about German culture and history.
Welcome to Germany, a country that celebrates precision, even among friends enjoying an evening out. Splitting the bill evenly is not an idea that has taken off here. Nor is buying each other rounds the same generous gesture it is in other countries.
For visitors accustomed to everyone paying an equal share – or taking tuns at the bar – this item-by-item accounting can feel strangely formal. And in a country with such a celebrated beer culture, it raises an obvious question: why don't Germans buy each other drinks?
This unspoken rule applies even in the most casual situations. In carefree Berlin, summer evenings often see younger people skipping a night of bar hopping in favour of gathering outside a Späti (late-night convenience store). Even when one person heads inside to buy the next round of drinks, don't assume generosity has replaced arithmetic.
"People will be counting who has paid how many rounds, most definitely," says Julian Berger, bartender at Orania Berlin , a luxury hotel in the city's edgy Kreuzberg district.
Dr Harald Pitters , an Austrian trend researcher who is married to a German, says the instinct is rooted in fairness and a desire to keep control of the situation. He has also seen how uncertainty can make buying rounds uncomfortable. "Two of my best friends are German, and this was always a point of contention when we went out together," he says.
"They didn't like the idea of rounds when there was no certainty around how long we would stay and how many rounds we would have. If everyone pays their way there is no room for disappointment."
"Germans have a very strong sense of justice," Berger adds. "They feel more comfortable if everyone pays for themselves. They don't like it when there is an imbalance."
In other words, keeping the bill clear is not necessarily seen as ungenerous. It can be a way of protecting the friendship. There is even a German saying that sums up this mentality: " Klare Rechnung, gute Freunde " (clear accounts, good friends).
As with any practice, however, there are exceptions to the rule. In the Biergärten (beer gardens) in southern Germany, where the standard drink is a one-litre mug of beer, rounds are more common. In fact, it is in the country's more traditional areas, including Bavaria, that you are more likely to see friends buying drinks for each other.
This is particularly true at traditional community festivals, which Pittars says are enjoying a revival among young people.

"At an Erntedankfest [harvest festival, where beer is the standard drink], it is very usual to buy rounds. You would out yourself as very uptight if you just bought a drink for you and your partner," he says. "That also applies at Karneval [Carnival] in Cologne or Hafengeburtstag [Port Anniversary] in Hamburg – any communal event involving drinking and dancing."
So what should visitors do? Berger advises assuming that everyone will pay their own way – unless someone makes it clear otherwise.
"If you are out with someone and they say, " Ich lade dich ein " [I am inviting you], that means they are paying," he says.
And there is no need to feel awkward about asking the waiter to split the bill, either. Most will automatically ask, " Getrennt oder zusammen? " (separately or together).
For many Germans, the natural answer remains: " Getrennt, bitte " (separately, please).
